posts.note: Guest essay by Jon Rosenberg (Part III). The author's own text is the intro, the closing thanks, and two footnotes; none contains a forecast. Jon's personal expectation of a future depressive episode is his own claim, not adopted by the author, and was not logged.

Interview with Kyle McAndrews (ex-CFO, Wave Neuroscience). Kyle's answers are his own and contain no forecasts. The author's forecasts are in his 'Request for Startups' answer on brain stimulation, plus two newsletter-plan items. Generic payer-behavior descriptions ('they're gonna be skeptical') were treated as present-state analysis and not logged.
Review of TMS/tDCS meta-analyses in Parkinson's disease plus an Ampa Health device announcement. 'We need better-designed studies' is normative and was not logged.
Retrospective analysis of the author's LinkedIn metrics. Only the two conditional takeaways about future post performance were logged; the rest is past analysis or advice.
Review of TMS-in-pregnancy evidence (Angeline et al. 2025) and the Early-TMS RCT protocol; plus a RAMHT '25 event plug.
Event announcement for RAMHT LA, May 18, 2025. All items are own-event statements; coder will likely mark CONTROL.
Satirical Sauron-as-founder monologue (April 1). The fictional voice contains no sincere world forecast; only the sincere RAMHT event aside at the end was logged.

statements.quote: There are four major domains of brain stimulation that are going to bear tremendous fruit.
statements.context: The author's answer to Kyle McAndrews' 'Request for Startups' question about the most promising approaches to brain health. He sets psychedelics aside and asserts that brain stimulation will deliver; he then walks through circuit-based TMS, low-dose electrical stimulation devices, and transcranial focused ultrasound.
statements.note: Headline call for the section; the specific sub-claims are logged separately.

statements.quote: now we have the opportunity to treat movement disorders, obsessive compulsive disorder, post traumatic stress disorder, bipolar depression, anxiety, dementia, insomnia, chronic pain, and addiction. It is an explosive array of treatments that are rapidly becoming possible.
statements.context: First domain: brain-circuit-based TMS guided by fMRI. The author claims circuit science will expand TMS beyond depression to a long list of indications and that these treatments are rapidly becoming possible.
statements.note: Compound claim across many indications; no dates.

statements.quote: We've already seen many of these devices come to market for things like migraine headache, and more are coming for depression, PTSD, and other disorders of the brain.
statements.context: Second domain: low-dose electrical (rather than magnetic) neuromodulation devices that are non-invasive, lightweight, inexpensive and home-deployable. The author expects more such devices to reach the market for depression, PTSD and other brain disorders.
statements.note: Market entry of medical devices implies clearance; could also be coded company_market. No company named.

statements.quote: None of this is in the clinical domain yet, it's still in research studies. However, the ability to wake humans up out of a coma by stimulating the thalamus seems extremely promising. So, to, the ability to address depression, or PTSD, deep in the brain, and with very limited risk.
statements.context: Third domain: transcranial focused ultrasound, described as 'very hard to ignore'. The author expects it to prove out for waking coma patients via thalamic stimulation and for treating depression or PTSD deep in the brain, while conceding it is research-stage only.
statements.note: Hedged; two indications in one statement.

statements.quote: The future is both now, and more is coming!
statements.context: Closing line of the brain-stimulation answer, after 'We have a range of interventions that are exciting. We have the ability to heal without causing unnecessary harm.' A general claim that more brain-stimulation interventions will arrive.
statements.note: Vague closing flourish; borderline truism. Logged for recall.

statements.quote: this is the first part, perhaps of many, of that conversation.
statements.context: Intro to the asynchronous interview with Kyle McAndrews. The author signals that further installments of the conversation may follow in the newsletter.
statements.note: Own newsletter plan; coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: Stay tuned for the next time Kyle McAndrews joins us for a chat.
statements.context: Sign-off of the interview post. The author asserts there will be a next conversation with Kyle McAndrews in the newsletter.

statements.quote: I hope better-designed devices that are easier to bring to patients will make a real difference—not just in depression, but especially in disorders where mobility is a serious barrier, like Parkinson’s Disease.
statements.context: After introducing Ampa Health's portable TMS device (co-founded by Jonathan Downar, now out of stealth), the author expects portable, easy-to-deploy TMS devices to matter for depression and especially for mobility-limited conditions like Parkinson's disease.
statements.note: Framed as hope; borderline wish with a predictive reading. Ampa is an author-affiliated company.

statements.quote: I’m thrilled to announce Ampa Health will be joining us at RAMHT ‘25 on May 18th in Los Angeles, right alongside the APA Annual Meeting.
statements.context: Event announcement: Ampa Health will appear at the author's Rapid Acting Mental Health Treatment (RAMHT) '25 event in Los Angeles on May 18, 2025, timed with the APA Annual Meeting.
statements.note: Own event; coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: The Ampa device isn’t cleared for the treatment of PD yet—no TMS treatment is. In order to get to that level of evidence, we will need design thinking—both for our devices and for our studies.
statements.context: Closing caveat of the Parkinson's post. The author notes no TMS device (including Ampa's) is cleared for Parkinson's disease and states what will be required to reach clearance-level evidence.
statements.note: Requirement claim with an implicit expectation of eventual clearance ('yet'); borderline. No date or probability.

statements.quote: If you write about deeply personal topics about what you're passionate, that's going do well on LinkedIn.
statements.context: First item of the 'Takeaways as I understand them' list closing the author's analysis of his LinkedIn engagement (7.7 percent engagement rate, 1m impressions a year). A conditional prediction about how personal posts perform on LinkedIn.
statements.note: Generic conditional advice derived from past data; borderline truism, low forecast value. Logged for recall.

statements.quote: Thank goodness we have one more RCT coming this year that didn't make it into the above review because it hasn’t been done yet.
statements.context: After reviewing Angeline et al. (2025), which found only three studies of TMS in pregnant women with MDD, the author points to the Early-TMS randomized trial (Becker-Sadzio et al. protocol, published February 2025) comparing rTMS/iTBS with SSRIs, and says it is coming this year.
statements.confidence_phrase: we have one more RCT coming
statements.note: Timing claim about a trial; whether 'coming' means readout or conduct is ambiguous.

statements.quote: the following RCT protocol was published before the trial is concluded, which I hope will meaningfully answer more of the most important questions we have about what to do for women who are pregnant and depressed
statements.context: Introducing the Early-TMS protocol ('Effectiveness of rTMS compared to SSRI as early treatment of depression'). The author expects the trial to answer key questions about treating depression in pregnancy.
statements.note: Framed as hope; borderline wish with a predictive reading.

statements.quote: The authors will compare iTBS stimulation to SSRIs in pregnant women with depression to determine which is better ... I know which I’d be betting on, but we don’t have to rely on a gut check or hunches when we have empirical answers.
statements.context: On the Early-TMS RCT (iTBS versus SSRIs in pregnant women with depression). The author signals an implicit bet on the outcome; given the post's thesis that rTMS is the safest and an effective option, the implied pick is iTBS/rTMS over SSRIs. He does not name the pick.
statements.confidence_phrase: I know which I’d be betting on
statements.note: Implicit direction inferred from the post's argument; the author does not state the pick outright. Joined across a footnote marker.

statements.quote: Science will move forward. The one bet I’m willing to make? The science will absolutely LAP the payment models if we don’t raise all our voices to both our employers and elected representatives.
statements.context: Right after the Early-TMS discussion. The author bets that the science of rTMS for depression in pregnancy will outrun insurer payment models unless clinicians lobby employers and legislators.
statements.note: Conditional ('if we don't raise all our voices'); explicitly framed as a bet.

statements.quote: And soon, thanks to the Early-TMS trial, we will have a direct comparison.
statements.context: Bottom line of the post: rTMS is the only biological treatment for depression in pregnancy with no known risk 'for now', and the Early-TMS trial will soon give a direct rTMS-versus-SSRI comparison.
statements.note: Restates the 'one more RCT coming this year' claim with a 'soon' horizon.
